panels.title: Network modes at a glance
panels.body:
bridge (default)   Container gets its own IP on docker0
                   Isolated from host; containers talk via bridge
                   Port publish: -p host:container adds iptables DNAT rule

host               Container shares host network namespace
                   No isolation; max performance; no -p needed
                   Risk: port conflicts, no network isolation

none               No network interface except loopback
                   Fully isolated; used for batch/offline jobs

overlay            Multi-host networking (Docker Swarm)
                   VXLAN tunnel between hosts; containers on any
                   node reach each other by service name

macvlan            Container gets its own MAC + IP on physical LAN
                   Appears as a physical device to the network
                   Useful for legacy apps expecting a real IP

panels.title: Container DNS — how 'db' resolves to an IP
panels.body:
User-defined bridge networks include Docker's embedded DNS:

  docker network create my-net
  docker run --name db --network my-net postgres
  docker run --name web --network my-net myapp

  Inside web: curl http://db:5432  ← resolves via Docker DNS
  Docker DNS reads the container name → returns its bridge IP

Default bridge (docker0) does NOT support DNS by name.
Always create a user-defined network for multi-container apps.

panels.title: Port publishing: -p vs --network host
pros: -p 8080:3000: explicit mapping, can run multiple containers on different host ports, security boundary maintained
--network host: zero overhead (no NAT/iptables), best for high-throughput services or when latency matters
cons: -p 8080:3000: iptables rules add ~10-30μs per packet; can't bind to host port 80 without root or CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
--network host: no isolation — a compromised container can reach all host ports; port conflicts possible
